blocks.text: …out and about safely

All notes from the chapter LEASH WORK apply as a matter of principle. Loose-leash walking in the city requires reliably learned procedures from LEASH WORK and their flexible, compromise-ready application depending on the respective stage of training.

The dog is always led on the same side. The leash is held mainly at its end, or at least so long that it hangs slack and loose. A leash hanging loosely is not a sign of loss of control – it is the sign of successful communication.
Loose-leash walking is the product of relaxation and security – the handler must bring both first before the dog can learn them.
Basic rules in detail 📋

We walk at a calm pace and always slightly slower than the dog would like to go. This deliberate slowing down signals to the dog who sets the pace, and is one of the most effective and least conspicuous gestures of leadership there is.

With a dog led on the left, we preferably walk on the right of the path – this way we draw the dog away from the distracting edges of the path. With a dog led on the right, we walk on the left of the path – this also spares oncoming traffic.

We radiate calm all round. We speak calmly and thereby convey to the dog that there is no danger. Praise is given with a calm voice and soothing stroking – no excited, effusive reaction that activates the dog again.
As an exception, the leash may be held shorter if otherwise bystanders would be bothered or endangered, or if the exercise requires it.
Exceptions to leading on one side are narrow, dangerous or surprising situations in which we must react spontaneously and safely.
The city from the dog’s point of view 🏙️

Urban areas are fundamentally to be regarded as very exciting for our dog. Noises, smells, people, vehicles, other animals, reflections, unfamiliar objects – the flood of stimuli in the city, in its density and unpredictability, can hardly be compared for a dog with what he experiences in open nature.

Our dog cannot classify this environment cognitively as we do. He relies entirely on our reaction as his point of orientation. If we are tense, he assumes that tension is appropriate. If we are calm, calm is appropriate. This transfer is not a metaphor – it is neurobiological reality.
To achieve calm movement through the city, it takes consistent leadership, calmness at the same time, and confident presence. These three things do not exclude each other – they depend on each other.

Strong insecurity in the handler can turn, in the dog, into unwanted forward reactions, avoidance behaviour or excessive arousal. In that moment, the dog tries to take matters into his own hands – because he senses that no one else is doing so.

The more often we move in urban areas, the greater the potential for calm and routine becomes. Habituation is a powerful tool – for the dog as well as for the dog handler. Anyone who becomes more confident in dealing with urban situations transfers this confidence directly to the dog.

What has a decisive effect here, above all, is our calm movement patterns and a relaxed tone of voice – regardless of the situation at hand. The dog does not judge us by our thoughts, but by our body and our voice.
Leash types and their significance 🔗
A standard leash of 1.5 to 2 m in length is the suitable starting point. It gives the dog enough room without taking control away from us.

Retractable leashes – so-called flexi leashes – are unsuitable for training loose-leash walking. Through their constant tension, they suggest to the dog that pulling on the leash is normal and without consequence. In addition, the dog handler is left without any sensitive means of communication. Anyone who wants to train loose-leash walking leaves the flexi leash at home.

The collar is sufficient for most training situations. Dogs that pull strongly or have a sensitive trachea benefit from a well-fitted chest harness – however, it should be known that chest harnesses, by their construction, tend to encourage rather than inhibit pulling. Anyone who chooses a harness does so deliberately and compensates through correspondingly precise leadership work.
Structure and layout of training rounds 🗺️

At first, we choose rather quiet streets with below-average encounter traffic. Time of day and day of the week play a greater role than is often thought: a shopping street early on a Saturday morning is a completely different learning environment from the same street at Saturday midday.
We divide our rounds so that we pass at least one free zone – an open area, green space or natural area in which the dog can shift down a gear.

An ideal route begins with quiet sections, leads into a free zone, then passes through busier zones and optionally ends with a further free zone. This alternating principle is a necessity of training physiology – continuous load without a break leads to lasting learning success neither in humans nor in dogs.

As learning progresses, we become increasingly independent of this strict sequence. At some point every walk will naturally be calm – deliberate planning is then only an occasional tool for new or particularly challenging environments.
We take note, in our heads – or even in practice – of which places and situations repeatedly occupy our dog. These points are not problems but training opportunities that we can deliberately repeat.
Procedure and objective 🦮

We always keep the leash loose and long. As soon as the leash is about to tighten, we bring the dog into the sit or down. We wait until he turns to us, and in doing so calmly walk a few steps backwards – this gently draws the dog’s attention back to us without creating pressure.

The first metres of each round can be tough and laborious at first. It is precisely here, however, that the course is set for everything that follows. A dog that learns in the first two minutes that pulling does not lead to the goal is a different dog at the start of the second hour.

Remember: The calmer, more confident and more precise this step is carried out over time, the more lasting the result. The dog’s form on the day must always be taken into account – on an agitated day, the demands are to be adjusted accordingly. Patience is not a sign of weakness but of understanding.

A change of side by the dog is to be corrected immediately: we stop, calmly bring the dog back to the desired side, have him sit or lie down, and only continue calmly once he has clearly settled. This reaction must always be the same – not strict, but reliable. Reliability is what gives the dog orientation in the long term.

In the free zone, where possible, we let the long trailing line run out or take the dog completely off the leash. Extensive play and romping is expressly desired – afterwards we continue relaxed and composed. The free zone is not a deserved conclusion but a built-in regulation tool within the training session.

We give praise exclusively in relaxed moments, when the dog is mentally with us. Praise at a moment when the dog is distracted or excited reinforces precisely this state. Calm praise in a calm moment, by contrast, makes calm moments attractive.
Encounters with people and other dogs 🐕
Encounters in urban space are the most frequent challenge of loose-leash walking and at the same time the greatest training resource.

When encounters with people are imminent, we react early, before our dog reacts. We bring him into the sit, let the encounter pass and continue calmly. In doing so, we do not seek eye contact with strangers, which would activate our dog further.

When encountering other dogs, we distinguish three cases: the other dog is on a leash and calm – we pass at as great a distance as possible. The other dog is on a leash and agitated – we cross to the other side of the street without hesitating. The other dog is running free – we bring our dog into the down, position ourselves between him and the strange dog and wait until the situation resolves.
An encounter does not have to take place just because it would be possible. We decide when and whether our dog has contact – not chance and not the other dog.
Important rules of conduct ⚠️

Absolutely avoid being out and about in the city with the dog stressed and excited. Anyone who notices that, on a particular day, they cannot muster the necessary calm shortens the round and goes home earlier.
Avoid strong distraction on our side – in particular looking at the smartphone during training. Our full attention belongs to the dog.
Avoid loud communication and hectic action with the dog. The voice is a means of leadership – and a calm one is more effective than a loud one.
Avoid impatience in any form. A short, calm walk is more valuable for learning progress than a long, tense training session.
Avoid the use of flexi leashes in training. They undermine every bit of learning progress in loose-leash walking.
Practical impulse: You set the pace

The most effective and least used lever of loose-leash walking is deliberate slowing down. On your next walk today, deliberately walk more slowly than your dog would like – and observe how he orients himself to you. No command, no jerking on the leash. Just pace. You will be surprised.
→ Do I consistently lead my dog on the same side?
→ Is my leash loose and long enough to allow a natural slack?
→ Do I deliberately walk slightly slower than my dog would like to go?
→ Do I react to tension on the leash immediately and uniformly with sit or down?
→ Have I deliberately planned my route with quiet sections and free zones?
→ Do I praise exclusively in calm, relaxed moments?
→ Do I remain early, calm and predictable during encounters?
→ Am I relaxed myself and free of hurry and distraction?
→ Do I adjust my demands to my dog’s form on the day?
→ Do I end every session with a positive, calm moment?
